By John Seiler (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/john-seiler/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 11:20 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California needs serious solutions to its housing crunch. Two bonds on the Nov. 3 ballot are not among them.
Proposition 1 is the $11.25 billion Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act. The Legislature put it on the ballot by passing Senate Bill 417, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed. The name is somewhat misleading because only $1.25 billion, or 11%, would go to veterans, a group most people want to help. The veterans themselves would repay the loans.
The remaining $10 billion, or 89%, would go to a grab bag of seven bureaucratic housing programs. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, this part would be repaid at a cost of $500 million to $600 million annually from the general fund — that is, by the taxpayers. For decades I’ve insisted: Bonds are delayed tax increases.
The largest allocation is $7.2 billion to “acquire, build or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings.” Then follow $1.1 billion to promote homeownership for low- and moderate-income households, $500 million for infrastructure programs, $450 million for farmworker housing, $350 million for student housing at UC and Cal State campuses, $200 million for tribal housing and $200 million for local pilot programs.
It’s clear the money is just is being divvied up to the most powerful special interests.
A big problem is the new bond spending would do nothing to alleviate the “fragmented and cumbersome” system the LAO called out in a March 2026 recommendation, “Streamlining California’s Affordable Housing Funding System.”
Proposition 37 is called the Middle-Class Homeownership Act by its sponsor, former Democratic Assembly Speaker and Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg. It could issue up to $25 billion in bonds for housing. The bonds would be paid back by the homeowners.
It would give buyers a state loan covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price. It’s a “second mortgage” because it sits behind their main mortgage, filling the down-payment gap. The homeowners would have to pay 3% of the price.
More than 900,000 signatures were gathered, far more than the 546,651 needed to put it on the ballot. The bond is “aimed specifically at brand-new construction for ownership housing for the middle class,” Hertzberg told Planning Report. He said young people, especially, “can’t come up with $150,000 or $200,000” for a down payment and have low FICO credit scores.
The LAO’s analysis of Proposition 37 found no direct state or local costs to taxpayers. The bondholders would take the hit on defaults. But the LAO cautions the actual results of the bond are “unknown,” including investor response, the cost to homebuyers versus other programs and whether it actually will increase homeownership.
For both Proposition 1 and Proposition 37, the greater problem is they could increase demand faster than supply, actually increasing the price of housing. That would put the cost of buying a home further out of reach for those not lucky enough to get these and other state programs.
Moreover, the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley tallied nearly 100 new laws touching “virtually all aspects of housing” passed by the Legislature since 2017. It would make sense to wait a few years to see how all these changes actually affect real housing and real families.
The state instead should direct its attention to the other aspect of affordability: the income levels needed to pay for the housing. Just this year, the Legislature passed and Newsom signed into law what the California Taxpayers Association branded “the largest tax increase” in state history.
That included new taxes on health care providers and software downloads. Friends of mine in small business, the heart of the middle class, are wondering how they will pay the new levies.
The new taxes were on top of the old taxes. The Tax Foundation calculates the Golden State’s top income tax rate of 14.6% is the highest in the nation. The average sales tax rate is 8.99%, below Louisiana’s nation-leading 10.11%. But the gas tax is the highest, at 70.92 cents a gallon.
What good is “affordable” housing if you can’t afford it?
Seiler, a U-T Opinion contributor, wrote this for the Southern California News Group.

By John Seiler (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/john-seiler/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 11:20 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California needs serious solutions to its housing crunch. Two bonds on the Nov. 3 ballot are not among them.
Proposition 1 is the $11.25 billion Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act. The Legislature put it on the ballot by passing Senate Bill 417, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed. The name is somewhat misleading because only $1.25 billion, or 11%, would go to veterans, a group most people want to help. The veterans themselves would repay the loans.
The remaining $10 billion, or 89%, would go to a grab bag of seven bureaucratic housing programs. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, this part would be repaid at a cost of $500 million to $600 million annually from the general fund — that is, by the taxpayers. For decades I’ve insisted: Bonds are delayed tax increases.
The largest allocation is $7.2 billion to “acquire, build or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings.” Then follow $1.1 billion to promote homeownership for low- and moderate-income households, $500 million for infrastructure programs, $450 million for farmworker housing, $350 million for student housing at UC and Cal State campuses, $200 million for tribal housing and $200 million for local pilot programs.
It’s clear the money is just is being divvied up to the most powerful special interests.
A big problem is the new bond spending would do nothing to alleviate the “fragmented and cumbersome” system the LAO called out in a March 2026 recommendation, “Streamlining California’s Affordable Housing Funding System.”
Proposition 37 is called the Middle-Class Homeownership Act by its sponsor, former Democratic Assembly Speaker and Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg. It could issue up to $25 billion in bonds for housing. The bonds would be paid back by the homeowners.
It would give buyers a state loan covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price. It’s a “second mortgage” because it sits behind their main mortgage, filling the down-payment gap. The homeowners would have to pay 3% of the price.
More than 900,000 signatures were gathered, far more than the 546,651 needed to put it on the ballot. The bond is “aimed specifically at brand-new construction for ownership housing for the middle class,” Hertzberg told Planning Report. He said young people, especially, “can’t come up with $150,000 or $200,000” for a down payment and have low FICO credit scores.
The LAO’s analysis of Proposition 37 found no direct state or local costs to taxpayers. The bondholders would take the hit on defaults. But the LAO cautions the actual results of the bond are “unknown,” including investor response, the cost to homebuyers versus other programs and whether it actually will increase homeownership.
For both Proposition 1 and Proposition 37, the greater problem is they could increase demand faster than supply, actually increasing the price of housing. That would put the cost of buying a home further out of reach for those not lucky enough to get these and other state programs.
Moreover, the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley tallied nearly 100 new laws touching “virtually all aspects of housing” passed by the Legislature since 2017. It would make sense to wait a few years to see how all these changes actually affect real housing and real families.
The state instead should direct its attention to the other aspect of affordability: the income levels needed to pay for the housing. Just this year, the Legislature passed and Newsom signed into law what the California Taxpayers Association branded “the largest tax increase” in state history.
That included new taxes on health care providers and software downloads. Friends of mine in small business, the heart of the middle class, are wondering how they will pay the new levies.
The new taxes were on top of the old taxes. The Tax Foundation calculates the Golden State’s top income tax rate of 14.6% is the highest in the nation. The average sales tax rate is 8.99%, below Louisiana’s nation-leading 10.11%. But the gas tax is the highest, at 70.92 cents a gallon.
What good is “affordable” housing if you can’t afford it?
Seiler, a U-T Opinion contributor, wrote this for the Southern California News Group.

Quick overview: Proposition 1
LAist's AirTalk host Larry Mantle's ballot cram session gets you ready to vote with guests Michael Alvarez, of Caltech, Sara Sadhwani of Pomona College, and Lee E. Ohanian of UCLA and the Hoover Institution.
This measure asks voters to approve $11.25 billion in state bonds for various affordable housing strategies. The revenue would go toward the construction of new income-restricted apartments, supportive housing for tenants overcoming homelessness, mortgage assistance for veterans and a number of other programs.
What’s at stake?
According to recent U.S. Census Bureau statistics (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48945), about 54% of California renters officially qualify as “cost-burdened,” meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on rent. The only states with higher levels of rent burden are Florida and Nevada.
California needs to build about 1 million new homes (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/affordable-housing-units-setback-california) specifically for low-income residents, based on current statewide planning goals. Proposition 1 aims to speed up that process by raising money from bonds that would be repaid from the state’s general fund over the next 25 years.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) on the ballot:
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
A "no" vote means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
Understanding Prop. 1
Affordable housing units generally set rents at no more than 30% of a tenant’s income. That means they often do not generate enough rental income to be profitable for developers. That’s where public subsidies come in.
In recent years, California has put more funding toward creating low-cost housing. According to a recent state legislative analysis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), California has funded various affordable housing programs with $8 billion from the state’s general fund since 2019.
But some of those funding streams are now drying up.
A previous measure also called Proposition 1, passed by voters in 2018, approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veteran mortgage programs. Proposition 2, also from 2018, put $2 billion toward the creation of 7,000 supportive units for formerly unhoused tenants. Both funds are now depleted.
Those state funds have run out at a time when state lawmakers say California can no longer rely on Washington, D.C., to expand or continue federal affordable housing efforts. They argue Prop. 1 could make an immediate difference for an estimated 45,000 units that are in the construction pipeline but have yet to break ground due to a lack of gap financing.
Here’s what supporters say
In addition to helping low-income renters, formerly unhoused tenants and veterans, Proposition 1 proponents say the bond would also fund programs specifically designed to help college students, youth exiting foster care, farmworkers, tribal communities and low-income first-time homebuyers.
Notable endorsements: The coalition (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition) of Proposition 1 supporters includes the Southern California Association of Nonprofit Housing, the California Association of Veterans Service Agencies and the California Federation of Labor Unions.
Here’s what opponents say
There is no organized campaign against Proposition 1, but a handful of Republican state lawmakers voted against putting it on the ballot. State Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents coastal Orange County and pockets of L.A. County, said Proposition 1 has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation.” He said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness.”
Notable opposition: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a frequent critic of new California revenue proposals, opposes Proposition 1 in its election guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/). The group writes that bonds rely on borrowed money, and debt service costs add up over time. "When used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget," the Howard Jarvis guide says.
Potential financial impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) repayment of the Proposition 1 bonds would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for the next 25 years.
Because bonds would need to be repaid with interest, the legislative analysis said costs would likely end up about 15% higher than if the state paid for the programs with existing funding.
In total, the analysis said Proposition 1 would provide subsidies for an estimated 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 college student beds and would help up to 40,000 households achieve homeownership, including about 2,100 veterans.

What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. By John Seiler (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/john-seiler/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 11:20 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California needs serious solutions to its housing crunch. Two bonds on the Nov. 3 ballot are not among them.
Proposition 1 is the $11.25 billion Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act. The Legislature put it on the ballot by passing Senate Bill 417, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed. The name is somewhat misleading because only $1.25 billion, or 11%, would go to veterans, a group most people want to help. The veterans themselves would repay the loans.
The remaining $10 billion, or 89%, would go to a grab bag of seven bureaucratic housing programs. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, this part would be repaid at a cost of $500 million to $600 million annually from the general fund — that is, by the taxpayers. For decades I’ve insisted: Bonds are delayed tax increases.
The largest allocation is $7.2 billion to “acquire, build or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings.” Then follow $1.1 billion to promote homeownership for low- and moderate-income households, $500 million for infrastructure programs, $450 million for farmworker housing, $350 million for student housing at UC and Cal State campuses, $200 million for tribal housing and $200 million for local pilot programs.
It’s clear the money is just is being divvied up to the most powerful special interests.
A big problem is the new bond spending would do nothing to alleviate the “fragmented and cumbersome” system the LAO called out in a March 2026 recommendation, “Streamlining California’s Affordable Housing Funding System.”
Proposition 37 is called the Middle-Class Homeownership Act by its sponsor, former Democratic Assembly Speaker and Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg. It could issue up to $25 billion in bonds for housing. The bonds would be paid back by the homeowners.
It would give buyers a state loan covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price. It’s a “second mortgage” because it sits behind their main mortgage, filling the down-payment gap. The homeowners would have to pay 3% of the price.
More than 900,000 signatures were gathered, far more than the 546,651 needed to put it on the ballot. The bond is “aimed specifically at brand-new construction for ownership housing for the middle class,” Hertzberg told Planning Report. He said young people, especially, “can’t come up with $150,000 or $200,000” for a down payment and have low FICO credit scores.
The LAO’s analysis of Proposition 37 found no direct state or local costs to taxpayers. The bondholders would take the hit on defaults. But the LAO cautions the actual results of the bond are “unknown,” including investor response, the cost to homebuyers versus other programs and whether it actually will increase homeownership.
For both Proposition 1 and Proposition 37, the greater problem is they could increase demand faster than supply, actually increasing the price of housing. That would put the cost of buying a home further out of reach for those not lucky enough to get these and other state programs.
Moreover, the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley tallied nearly 100 new laws touching “virtually all aspects of housing” passed by the Legislature since 2017. It would make sense to wait a few years to see how all these changes actually affect real housing and real families.
The state instead should direct its attention to the other aspect of affordability: the income levels needed to pay for the housing. Just this year, the Legislature passed and Newsom signed into law what the California Taxpayers Association branded “the largest tax increase” in state history.
That included new taxes on health care providers and software downloads. Friends of mine in small business, the heart of the middle class, are wondering how they will pay the new levies.
The new taxes were on top of the old taxes. The Tax Foundation calculates the Golden State’s top income tax rate of 14.6% is the highest in the nation. The average sales tax rate is 8.99%, below Louisiana’s nation-leading 10.11%. But the gas tax is the highest, at 70.92 cents a gallon.
What good is “affordable” housing if you can’t afford it?
Seiler, a U-T Opinion contributor, wrote this for the Southern California News Group.

Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Opponents have not reported receiving any contributions. READ NEXT California has 40,000 affordable housing units ready to break ground. NO on Prop. 1
Called the “Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” this is $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds with only $1.25 billion allocated to benefit veterans. The rest will finance other housing assistance programs. Bonds are borrowed money. Like all general obligation bonds, the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest that must be paid to investors. Bonds are the most expensive way to pay for anything, and when used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget.
Vote NO on 1 .
NO on Prop. 2
This measure makes changes to the Gann Limit, passed by voters in 1979, and to the rules for the Budget Stabilization Account (“Rainy Day Fund”) that were approved by voters in 2014. Tax revenue goes up and down in California with the stock market, because of the state’s dependence on taxes from high earners and capital gains. Proposition 2 attempts to address this revenue volatility challenge with new rules for the Budget Stabilization Account. However, while Prop. 2 addresses the treatment of appropriations into and out of reserve funds in a way that makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility, it doesn’t address the weakening of the Gann Limit by Propositions 98 (1988) and 111 (1990), enabling reckless overspending that has led to structural deficits and self-inflicted budget “emergencies.” California is in desperate need of fiscal discipline. The changes in the state constitution that permit unlimited spending should be reversed. Prop. 2 falls far short of real spending reform and, unfortunately, amounts to little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb.
Vote NO on 2 .
NO on Prop. 3
Remember the “temporary” income tax rate hike “for the schools” that was passed in 2012 and “temporarily” renewed in 2016? This measure renews it again and this time makes it permanent. California has the highest income tax rates in the nation, and every year the state has a bigger budget and a higher cost of living to show for it. These “temporary” income tax rate hikes should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases.
Vote NO on 3 .
NO on Prop. 4
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974 (PRA), prohibits the use of tax money to finance political campaigns for elective office. Proposition 4 would remove that ban. HJTA has previously won court cases upholding this provision of the PRA, and we haven’t changed our position. Taxpayers should not have to pay the campaign expenses of candidates running for office or incumbents running for re-election.
Vote NO on 4 .
NO on Prop. 5
This measure alters the constitutional right to recall a state officer and vote for a replacement candidate. Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate in recalls of statewide officeholders and state legislators. Offices would be filled by appointment or later special election. If a governor was recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term or until a special election, depending on timing. Proposition 5 allows the recalled officeholder to run in the special election to fill the seat, which current law prohibits. This measure makes a mockery of the recall process.
Vote NO on 5 .
NO on Prop. 37
This measure authorizes $25 billion in bonds for a program that would offer second-mortgage loans for down payments on newly constructed or converted homes (not existing homes) to eligible buyers who earn less than 200% of the area median income. Although there is no direct cost to taxpayers, a market downturn could cause mass foreclosures if stretched borrowers are unable to make their payments or sell the home for what they owe. Investors bear the financial risks, but the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) must manage this massive pool of funds to protect the bondholders and pay them the interest they are owed. HJTA appreciates the intent of this measure, but we have concerns about the size of the program and the criteria for eligibility to participate. Prop. 37 is not a constitutional amendment, which leaves it subject to legislative alteration. More fundamentally, California’s housing crisis is better addressed with less government impediments to building rather than a new government program. We urge a No vote.
Vote NO on 37 .
NO on Prop. 38
Another bond measure, Proposition 38 authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for research and therapies related to using the body’s immune system to treat disease. There is no reason that this cost should be borne by California taxpayers. Viable research can be funded by pharmaceutical companies, foundations and the federal government. An analysis by CalMatters reveals that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. Prop. 38 appears to be a clear case of self-dealing at the expense of taxpayers.
Vote NO on 38 .
YES on Prop. 39
Proposition 39 is the Voter ID initiative. While 36 states currently require some form of voter ID, California isn’t one of them. Voter ID is used successfully around the country to prevent voter impersonation at the polls and to ensure that mail ballots are validly submitted by eligible voters. It’s especially important to California taxpayers to secure our elections from the potential for fraud, because billions of dollars of tax measures are on the ballot in nearly every election.
Vote YES on 39 .
NO on Prop. 40
This is the “wealth tax,” supposedly affecting only billionaires but in fact a threat to every California taxpayer and homeowner. Proposition 40 imposes a “one-time tax” of 5% of “covered assets” valued above $1 billion. However, the measure includes language that allows the Legislature to rewrite the law later, potentially changing the thresholds, the assets that are covered, the percentage to be taken, and the number of times the tax would be levied. This is an entirely new type of tax, and we don’t know where it will lead. Will all Californians have to submit forms to the Franchise Tax Board declaring their assets every year? How much will ordinary Californians have to pay for “wealth tax preparation” to comply with this law?
Vote NO on 40 .
YES on Prop. 41
This measure requires pre-election audits of programs that would be funded by new statewide special taxes. It’s a good idea to find out where the existing funds are going before voters are asked to approve higher taxes for the same programs.
Vote YES on 41 .
YES on Prop. 42
In direct opposition to the “wealth tax,” this measure would prohibit any new state tax that taxes the ownership or control of personal property or applies retroactively based on activities or status that existed before the effective date of the new state tax. This will protect Californians, especially homeowners, from the risk of a “wealth tax” on the value of homes or any other accumulated savings and investments.
Vote YES on 42 .
YES on Prop. 43
Proposition 43 is the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 . It restores Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Prop. 43 closes the court-created “Upland” loophole that has allowed special interest groups to write their own tax increases, direct the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Because of this loophole, Californians are paying billions of dollars in taxes that they should not have had to pay.
Vote YES on 43 and tell a friend!
NO on Prop. 44
This measure requires community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services, not management and overhead. It authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance on qualifying expenditures and lets the Department of Public Health issue waivers. It authorizes monetary penalties and criminal charges. It is sponsored by a powerful labor organization seeking to expand its control over private clinics.
Vote NO on 44 .
YES on Prop. 45
Few things have impeded rational housing policy in the state more than the California Environmental Quality Act. It slows down development which, in turn, limits housing supply, increasing the cost of living. Far from being a tool to address legitimate environment concerns, it has been used more frequently as leverage by labor organizations to exact favorable labor agreements. While CEQA reform to prevent excessive delays is necessary, Proposition 45 is not perfect since it carves out only certain projects for reform and locks in costly labor agreements. It also creates opportunities for government to pick winners and losers. But while HJTA would prefer a full revamp of CEQA, Prop. 45 is a good first step.
Vote YES on 45 .
LOCAL BALLOT MEASURE RECOMMENDATIONS
City of Los Angeles
NO on Measure FD
This is a one-half percent sales tax increase in the city of L.A. with the revenue earmarked for the fire department. We oppose this measure because the sales tax in Los Angeles will already rise to 10.25% in October because of Measure ER passing in L.A. County in June, and because the City Council and the Mayor should fully fund the fire department from the existing budget of approximately $15 billion without a tax increase. This measure is a special tax that should require a two-thirds vote to pass, but courts have allowed “citizens’ initiative tax increases,” placed on the ballot by collecting signatures, to pass with fewer votes. HJTA’s ballot measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Proposition 43 on the November ballot) will close the loophole, but this tax increase, if approved by just 50% plus one vote, will squeeze through it before Proposition 43 takes effect in January.
City of Santa Monica
NO on Measure ES
This is a parcel tax, an extra $495 per taxable parcel of property every year, adjusted annually for inflation. The revenue is earmarked for schools. Special taxes are required by the constitution to be approved by two-thirds of voters, but this is another “citizens’ initiative tax increase” rushing to squeeze through the court-created “Upland” loophole before voters approve Proposition 43 in November.
City of Palos Verdes Estates
NO on Measure PVE
This is a renewal of a parcel tax with a massive increase in the per-parcel rate from $342 to $1,025 to pay for police services and “to pay down the City's unfunded accrued pension liability.” City voters previously rejected a different measure in June to renew and increase the temporary parcel tax.
El Dorado County
NO on Measure S
Measure S is a 30-year countywide sales tax increase. It would raise the sales tax by 3/8 percent. Marshall Medical Center is sponsoring the campaign for the tax. The Yes on S website states that “Marshall receives revenue to support $125M in bond issuance to fund capital improvements.” El Dorado County has only two hospitals: Marshall Medical Center and Barton Memorial Hospital. Measure S is structured so Marshall qualifies for the hospital funding while Barton does not. South Lake Tahoe residents would still pay the countywide tax even though Barton falls below the measure’s hospital eligibility threshold.
Five-County Bay Area
NO on regional transit sales tax
This is a sales tax increase of at least one-half percent (1% in San Francisco) in five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara) to fund transit. Critics rightly argue that the longstanding financial and management problems of transit systems in the Bay Area will not be fixed with another tax increase. Beyond that, a higher sales tax burdens people who already pay high sales taxes and are struggling with the high cost of living. This measure, too, is a “citizens’ initiative tax increase” attempting to get through the court-created loophole before HJTA closes it with Proposition 43.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? It is similar to last November’s County Proposition B, which garnered 62% of the support of the city voters and was endorsed by The Times.
Remember, the average cost increase to each homeowner is just $1.10 per month.

HJTA’S QUICK VOTING GUIDE

NO on Prop. 1
Called the “Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” this is $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds with only $1.25 billion allocated to benefit veterans. The rest will finance other housing assistance programs. Bonds are borrowed money. Like all general obligation bonds, the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest that must be paid to investors. Bonds are the most expensive way to pay for anything, and when used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget.
Vote NO on 1 .
NO on Prop. 2
This measure makes changes to the Gann Limit, passed by voters in 1979, and to the rules for the Budget Stabilization Account (“Rainy Day Fund”) that were approved by voters in 2014. Tax revenue goes up and down in California with the stock market, because of the state’s dependence on taxes from high earners and capital gains. Proposition 2 attempts to address this revenue volatility challenge with new rules for the Budget Stabilization Account. However, while Prop. 2 addresses the treatment of appropriations into and out of reserve funds in a way that makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility, it doesn’t address the weakening of the Gann Limit by Propositions 98 (1988) and 111 (1990), enabling reckless overspending that has led to structural deficits and self-inflicted budget “emergencies.” California is in desperate need of fiscal discipline. The changes in the state constitution that permit unlimited spending should be reversed. Prop. 2 falls far short of real spending reform and, unfortunately, amounts to little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb.
Vote NO on 2 .
NO on Prop. 3
Remember the “temporary” income tax rate hike “for the schools” that was passed in 2012 and “temporarily” renewed in 2016? This measure renews it again and this time makes it permanent. California has the highest income tax rates in the nation, and every year the state has a bigger budget and a higher cost of living to show for it. These “temporary” income tax rate hikes should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases.
Vote NO on 3 .
NO on Prop. 4
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974 (PRA), prohibits the use of tax money to finance political campaigns for elective office. Proposition 4 would remove that ban. HJTA has previously won court cases upholding this provision of the PRA, and we haven’t changed our position. Taxpayers should not have to pay the campaign expenses of candidates running for office or incumbents running for re-election.
Vote NO on 4 .
NO on Prop. 5
This measure alters the constitutional right to recall a state officer and vote for a replacement candidate. Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate in recalls of statewide officeholders and state legislators. Offices would be filled by appointment or later special election. If a governor was recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term or until a special election, depending on timing. Proposition 5 allows the recalled officeholder to run in the special election to fill the seat, which current law prohibits. This measure makes a mockery of the recall process.
Vote NO on 5 .
NO on Prop. 37
This measure authorizes $25 billion in bonds for a program that would offer second-mortgage loans for down payments on newly constructed or converted homes (not existing homes) to eligible buyers who earn less than 200% of the area median income. Although there is no direct cost to taxpayers, a market downturn could cause mass foreclosures if stretched borrowers are unable to make their payments or sell the home for what they owe. Investors bear the financial risks, but the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) must manage this massive pool of funds to protect the bondholders and pay them the interest they are owed. HJTA appreciates the intent of this measure, but we have concerns about the size of the program and the criteria for eligibility to participate. Prop. 37 is not a constitutional amendment, which leaves it subject to legislative alteration. More fundamentally, California’s housing crisis is better addressed with less government impediments to building rather than a new government program. We urge a No vote.
Vote NO on 37 .
NO on Prop. 38
Another bond measure, Proposition 38 authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for research and therapies related to using the body’s immune system to treat disease. There is no reason that this cost should be borne by California taxpayers. Viable research can be funded by pharmaceutical companies, foundations and the federal government. An analysis by CalMatters reveals that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. Prop. 38 appears to be a clear case of self-dealing at the expense of taxpayers.
Vote NO on 38 .
YES on Prop. 39
Proposition 39 is the Voter ID initiative. While 36 states currently require some form of voter ID, California isn’t one of them. Voter ID is used successfully around the country to prevent voter impersonation at the polls and to ensure that mail ballots are validly submitted by eligible voters. It’s especially important to California taxpayers to secure our elections from the potential for fraud, because billions of dollars of tax measures are on the ballot in nearly every election.
Vote YES on 39 .
NO on Prop. 40
This is the “wealth tax,” supposedly affecting only billionaires but in fact a threat to every California taxpayer and homeowner. Proposition 40 imposes a “one-time tax” of 5% of “covered assets” valued above $1 billion. However, the measure includes language that allows the Legislature to rewrite the law later, potentially changing the thresholds, the assets that are covered, the percentage to be taken, and the number of times the tax would be levied. This is an entirely new type of tax, and we don’t know where it will lead. Will all Californians have to submit forms to the Franchise Tax Board declaring their assets every year? How much will ordinary Californians have to pay for “wealth tax preparation” to comply with this law?
Vote NO on 40 .
YES on Prop. 41
This measure requires pre-election audits of programs that would be funded by new statewide special taxes. It’s a good idea to find out where the existing funds are going before voters are asked to approve higher taxes for the same programs.
Vote YES on 41 .
YES on Prop. 42
In direct opposition to the “wealth tax,” this measure would prohibit any new state tax that taxes the ownership or control of personal property or applies retroactively based on activities or status that existed before the effective date of the new state tax. This will protect Californians, especially homeowners, from the risk of a “wealth tax” on the value of homes or any other accumulated savings and investments.
Vote YES on 42 .
YES on Prop. 43
Proposition 43 is the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 . It restores Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Prop. 43 closes the court-created “Upland” loophole that has allowed special interest groups to write their own tax increases, direct the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Because of this loophole, Californians are paying billions of dollars in taxes that they should not have had to pay.
Vote YES on 43 and tell a friend!
NO on Prop. 44
This measure requires community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services, not management and overhead. It authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance on qualifying expenditures and lets the Department of Public Health issue waivers. It authorizes monetary penalties and criminal charges. It is sponsored by a powerful labor organization seeking to expand its control over private clinics.
Vote NO on 44 .
YES on Prop. 45
Few things have impeded rational housing policy in the state more than the California Environmental Quality Act. It slows down development which, in turn, limits housing supply, increasing the cost of living. Far from being a tool to address legitimate environment concerns, it has been used more frequently as leverage by labor organizations to exact favorable labor agreements. While CEQA reform to prevent excessive delays is necessary, Proposition 45 is not perfect since it carves out only certain projects for reform and locks in costly labor agreements. It also creates opportunities for government to pick winners and losers. But while HJTA would prefer a full revamp of CEQA, Prop. 45 is a good first step.
Vote YES on 45 .
LOCAL BALLOT MEASURE RECOMMENDATIONS
City of Los Angeles
NO on Measure FD
This is a one-half percent sales tax increase in the city of L.A. with the revenue earmarked for the fire department. We oppose this measure because the sales tax in Los Angeles will already rise to 10.25% in October because of Measure ER passing in L.A. County in June, and because the City Council and the Mayor should fully fund the fire department from the existing budget of approximately $15 billion without a tax increase. This measure is a special tax that should require a two-thirds vote to pass, but courts have allowed “citizens’ initiative tax increases,” placed on the ballot by collecting signatures, to pass with fewer votes. HJTA’s ballot measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Proposition 43 on the November ballot) will close the loophole, but this tax increase, if approved by just 50% plus one vote, will squeeze through it before Proposition 43 takes effect in January.
City of Santa Monica
NO on Measure ES
This is a parcel tax, an extra $495 per taxable parcel of property every year, adjusted annually for inflation. The revenue is earmarked for schools. Special taxes are required by the constitution to be approved by two-thirds of voters, but this is another “citizens’ initiative tax increase” rushing to squeeze through the court-created “Upland” loophole before voters approve Proposition 43 in November.
City of Palos Verdes Estates
NO on Measure PVE
This is a renewal of a parcel tax with a massive increase in the per-parcel rate from $342 to $1,025 to pay for police services and “to pay down the City's unfunded accrued pension liability.” City voters previously rejected a different measure in June to renew and increase the temporary parcel tax.
El Dorado County
NO on Measure S
Measure S is a 30-year countywide sales tax increase. It would raise the sales tax by 3/8 percent. Marshall Medical Center is sponsoring the campaign for the tax. The Yes on S website states that “Marshall receives revenue to support $125M in bond issuance to fund capital improvements.” El Dorado County has only two hospitals: Marshall Medical Center and Barton Memorial Hospital. Measure S is structured so Marshall qualifies for the hospital funding while Barton does not. South Lake Tahoe residents would still pay the countywide tax even though Barton falls below the measure’s hospital eligibility threshold.
Five-County Bay Area
NO on regional transit sales tax
This is a sales tax increase of at least one-half percent (1% in San Francisco) in five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara) to fund transit. Critics rightly argue that the longstanding financial and management problems of transit systems in the Bay Area will not be fixed with another tax increase. Beyond that, a higher sales tax burdens people who already pay high sales taxes and are struggling with the high cost of living. This measure, too, is a “citizens’ initiative tax increase” attempting to get through the court-created loophole before HJTA closes it with Proposition 43.

This is the “wealth tax,” supposedly affecting only billionaires but in fact a threat to every California taxpayer and homeowner. Proposition 40 imposes a “one-time tax” of 5% of “covered assets” valued above $1 billion. However, the measure includes language that allows the Legislature to rewrite the law later, potentially changing the thresholds, the assets that are covered, the percentage to be taken, and the number of times the tax would be levied. This is an entirely new type of tax, and we don’t know where it will lead. Will all Californians have to submit forms to the Franchise Tax Board declaring their assets every year? How much will ordinary Californians have to pay for “wealth tax preparation” to comply with this law?
Vote NO on 40 .
YES on Prop. 41
This measure requires pre-election audits of programs that would be funded by new statewide special taxes. It’s a good idea to find out where the existing funds are going before voters are asked to approve higher taxes for the same programs.
Vote YES on 41 .
YES on Prop. 42
In direct opposition to the “wealth tax,” this measure would prohibit any new state tax that taxes the ownership or control of personal property or applies retroactively based on activities or status that existed before the effective date of the new state tax. This will protect Californians, especially homeowners, from the risk of a “wealth tax” on the value of homes or any other accumulated savings and investments.
Vote YES on 42 .
YES on Prop. 43
Proposition 43 is the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 . It restores Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Prop. 43 closes the court-created “Upland” loophole that has allowed special interest groups to write their own tax increases, direct the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Because of this loophole, Californians are paying billions of dollars in taxes that they should not have had to pay.
Vote YES on 43 and tell a friend!
NO on Prop. 44
This measure requires community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services, not management and overhead. It authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance on qualifying expenditures and lets the Department of Public Health issue waivers. It authorizes monetary penalties and criminal charges. It is sponsored by a powerful labor organization seeking to expand its control over private clinics.
Vote NO on 44 .
YES on Prop. 45
Few things have impeded rational housing policy in the state more than the California Environmental Quality Act. It slows down development which, in turn, limits housing supply, increasing the cost of living. Far from being a tool to address legitimate environment concerns, it has been used more frequently as leverage by labor organizations to exact favorable labor agreements. While CEQA reform to prevent excessive delays is necessary, Proposition 45 is not perfect since it carves out only certain projects for reform and locks in costly labor agreements. It also creates opportunities for government to pick winners and losers. But while HJTA would prefer a full revamp of CEQA, Prop. 45 is a good first step.
Vote YES on 45 .
LOCAL BALLOT MEASURE RECOMMENDATIONS
City of Los Angeles
NO on Measure FD
This is a one-half percent sales tax increase in the city of L.A. with the revenue earmarked for the fire department. We oppose this measure because the sales tax in Los Angeles will already rise to 10.25% in October because of Measure ER passing in L.A. County in June, and because the City Council and the Mayor should fully fund the fire department from the existing budget of approximately $15 billion without a tax increase. This measure is a special tax that should require a two-thirds vote to pass, but courts have allowed “citizens’ initiative tax increases,” placed on the ballot by collecting signatures, to pass with fewer votes. HJTA’s ballot measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Proposition 43 on the November ballot) will close the loophole, but this tax increase, if approved by just 50% plus one vote, will squeeze through it before Proposition 43 takes effect in January.
City of Santa Monica
NO on Measure ES
This is a parcel tax, an extra $495 per taxable parcel of property every year, adjusted annually for inflation. The revenue is earmarked for schools. Special taxes are required by the constitution to be approved by two-thirds of voters, but this is another “citizens’ initiative tax increase” rushing to squeeze through the court-created “Upland” loophole before voters approve Proposition 43 in November.
City of Palos Verdes Estates
NO on Measure PVE
This is a renewal of a parcel tax with a massive increase in the per-parcel rate from $342 to $1,025 to pay for police services and “to pay down the City's unfunded accrued pension liability.” City voters previously rejected a different measure in June to renew and increase the temporary parcel tax.
El Dorado County
NO on Measure S
Measure S is a 30-year countywide sales tax increase. It would raise the sales tax by 3/8 percent. Marshall Medical Center is sponsoring the campaign for the tax. The Yes on S website states that “Marshall receives revenue to support $125M in bond issuance to fund capital improvements.” El Dorado County has only two hospitals: Marshall Medical Center and Barton Memorial Hospital. Measure S is structured so Marshall qualifies for the hospital funding while Barton does not. South Lake Tahoe residents would still pay the countywide tax even though Barton falls below the measure’s hospital eligibility threshold.
Five-County Bay Area
NO on regional transit sales tax
This is a sales tax increase of at least one-half percent (1% in San Francisco) in five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara) to fund transit. Critics rightly argue that the longstanding financial and management problems of transit systems in the Bay Area will not be fixed with another tax increase. Beyond that, a higher sales tax burdens people who already pay high sales taxes and are struggling with the high cost of living. This measure, too, is a “citizens’ initiative tax increase” attempting to get through the court-created loophole before HJTA closes it with Proposition 43.
