Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. By John Seiler (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/john-seiler/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 11:20 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California needs serious solutions to its housing crunch. Two bonds on the Nov. 3 ballot are not among them.
Proposition 1 is the $11.25 billion Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act. The Legislature put it on the ballot by passing Senate Bill 417, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed. The name is somewhat misleading because only $1.25 billion, or 11%, would go to veterans, a group most people want to help. The veterans themselves would repay the loans.
The remaining $10 billion, or 89%, would go to a grab bag of seven bureaucratic housing programs. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, this part would be repaid at a cost of $500 million to $600 million annually from the general fund — that is, by the taxpayers. For decades I’ve insisted: Bonds are delayed tax increases.
The largest allocation is $7.2 billion to “acquire, build or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings.” Then follow $1.1 billion to promote homeownership for low- and moderate-income households, $500 million for infrastructure programs, $450 million for farmworker housing, $350 million for student housing at UC and Cal State campuses, $200 million for tribal housing and $200 million for local pilot programs.
It’s clear the money is just is being divvied up to the most powerful special interests.
A big problem is the new bond spending would do nothing to alleviate the “fragmented and cumbersome” system the LAO called out in a March 2026 recommendation, “Streamlining California’s Affordable Housing Funding System.”
Proposition 37 is called the Middle-Class Homeownership Act by its sponsor, former Democratic Assembly Speaker and Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg. It could issue up to $25 billion in bonds for housing. The bonds would be paid back by the homeowners.
It would give buyers a state loan covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price. It’s a “second mortgage” because it sits behind their main mortgage, filling the down-payment gap. The homeowners would have to pay 3% of the price.
More than 900,000 signatures were gathered, far more than the 546,651 needed to put it on the ballot. The bond is “aimed specifically at brand-new construction for ownership housing for the middle class,” Hertzberg told Planning Report. He said young people, especially, “can’t come up with $150,000 or $200,000” for a down payment and have low FICO credit scores.
The LAO’s analysis of Proposition 37 found no direct state or local costs to taxpayers. The bondholders would take the hit on defaults. But the LAO cautions the actual results of the bond are “unknown,” including investor response, the cost to homebuyers versus other programs and whether it actually will increase homeownership.
For both Proposition 1 and Proposition 37, the greater problem is they could increase demand faster than supply, actually increasing the price of housing. That would put the cost of buying a home further out of reach for those not lucky enough to get these and other state programs.
Moreover, the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley tallied nearly 100 new laws touching “virtually all aspects of housing” passed by the Legislature since 2017. It would make sense to wait a few years to see how all these changes actually affect real housing and real families.
The state instead should direct its attention to the other aspect of affordability: the income levels needed to pay for the housing. Just this year, the Legislature passed and Newsom signed into law what the California Taxpayers Association branded “the largest tax increase” in state history.
That included new taxes on health care providers and software downloads. Friends of mine in small business, the heart of the middle class, are wondering how they will pay the new levies.
The new taxes were on top of the old taxes. The Tax Foundation calculates the Golden State’s top income tax rate of 14.6% is the highest in the nation. The average sales tax rate is 8.99%, below Louisiana’s nation-leading 10.11%. But the gas tax is the highest, at 70.92 cents a gallon.
What good is “affordable” housing if you can’t afford it?
Seiler, a U-T Opinion contributor, wrote this for the Southern California News Group.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Opponents have not reported receiving any contributions. READ NEXT California has 40,000 affordable housing units ready to break ground. HJTA’S QUICK VOTING GUIDE

NO on Prop. 1
Called the “Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” this is $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds with only $1.25 billion allocated to benefit veterans. The rest will finance other housing assistance programs. Bonds are borrowed money. Like all general obligation bonds, the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest that must be paid to investors. Bonds are the most expensive way to pay for anything, and when used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget.
Vote NO on 1 .
NO on Prop. 2
This measure makes changes to the Gann Limit, passed by voters in 1979, and to the rules for the Budget Stabilization Account (“Rainy Day Fund”) that were approved by voters in 2014. Tax revenue goes up and down in California with the stock market, because of the state’s dependence on taxes from high earners and capital gains. Proposition 2 attempts to address this revenue volatility challenge with new rules for the Budget Stabilization Account. However, while Prop. 2 addresses the treatment of appropriations into and out of reserve funds in a way that makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility, it doesn’t address the weakening of the Gann Limit by Propositions 98 (1988) and 111 (1990), enabling reckless overspending that has led to structural deficits and self-inflicted budget “emergencies.” California is in desperate need of fiscal discipline. The changes in the state constitution that permit unlimited spending should be reversed. Prop. 2 falls far short of real spending reform and, unfortunately, amounts to little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb.
Vote NO on 2 .
NO on Prop. 3
Remember the “temporary” income tax rate hike “for the schools” that was passed in 2012 and “temporarily” renewed in 2016? This measure renews it again and this time makes it permanent. California has the highest income tax rates in the nation, and every year the state has a bigger budget and a higher cost of living to show for it. These “temporary” income tax rate hikes should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases.
Vote NO on 3 .
NO on Prop. 4
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974 (PRA), prohibits the use of tax money to finance political campaigns for elective office. Proposition 4 would remove that ban. HJTA has previously won court cases upholding this provision of the PRA, and we haven’t changed our position. Taxpayers should not have to pay the campaign expenses of candidates running for office or incumbents running for re-election.
Vote NO on 4 .
NO on Prop. 5
This measure alters the constitutional right to recall a state officer and vote for a replacement candidate. Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate in recalls of statewide officeholders and state legislators. Offices would be filled by appointment or later special election. If a governor was recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term or until a special election, depending on timing. Proposition 5 allows the recalled officeholder to run in the special election to fill the seat, which current law prohibits. This measure makes a mockery of the recall process.
Vote NO on 5 .
NO on Prop. 37
This measure authorizes $25 billion in bonds for a program that would offer second-mortgage loans for down payments on newly constructed or converted homes (not existing homes) to eligible buyers who earn less than 200% of the area median income. Although there is no direct cost to taxpayers, a market downturn could cause mass foreclosures if stretched borrowers are unable to make their payments or sell the home for what they owe. Investors bear the financial risks, but the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) must manage this massive pool of funds to protect the bondholders and pay them the interest they are owed. HJTA appreciates the intent of this measure, but we have concerns about the size of the program and the criteria for eligibility to participate. Prop. 37 is not a constitutional amendment, which leaves it subject to legislative alteration. More fundamentally, California’s housing crisis is better addressed with less government impediments to building rather than a new government program. We urge a No vote.
Vote NO on 37 .
NO on Prop. 38
Another bond measure, Proposition 38 authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for research and therapies related to using the body’s immune system to treat disease. There is no reason that this cost should be borne by California taxpayers. Viable research can be funded by pharmaceutical companies, foundations and the federal government. An analysis by CalMatters reveals that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. Prop. 38 appears to be a clear case of self-dealing at the expense of taxpayers.
Vote NO on 38 .
YES on Prop. 39
Proposition 39 is the Voter ID initiative. While 36 states currently require some form of voter ID, California isn’t one of them. Voter ID is used successfully around the country to prevent voter impersonation at the polls and to ensure that mail ballots are validly submitted by eligible voters. It’s especially important to California taxpayers to secure our elections from the potential for fraud, because billions of dollars of tax measures are on the ballot in nearly every election.
Vote YES on 39 .
NO on Prop. 40
This is the “wealth tax,” supposedly affecting only billionaires but in fact a threat to every California taxpayer and homeowner. Proposition 40 imposes a “one-time tax” of 5% of “covered assets” valued above $1 billion. However, the measure includes language that allows the Legislature to rewrite the law later, potentially changing the thresholds, the assets that are covered, the percentage to be taken, and the number of times the tax would be levied. This is an entirely new type of tax, and we don’t know where it will lead. Will all Californians have to submit forms to the Franchise Tax Board declaring their assets every year? How much will ordinary Californians have to pay for “wealth tax preparation” to comply with this law?
Vote NO on 40 .
YES on Prop. 41
This measure requires pre-election audits of programs that would be funded by new statewide special taxes. It’s a good idea to find out where the existing funds are going before voters are asked to approve higher taxes for the same programs.
Vote YES on 41 .
YES on Prop. 42
In direct opposition to the “wealth tax,” this measure would prohibit any new state tax that taxes the ownership or control of personal property or applies retroactively based on activities or status that existed before the effective date of the new state tax. This will protect Californians, especially homeowners, from the risk of a “wealth tax” on the value of homes or any other accumulated savings and investments.
Vote YES on 42 .
YES on Prop. 43
Proposition 43 is the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 . It restores Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Prop. 43 closes the court-created “Upland” loophole that has allowed special interest groups to write their own tax increases, direct the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Because of this loophole, Californians are paying billions of dollars in taxes that they should not have had to pay.
Vote YES on 43 and tell a friend!
NO on Prop. 44
This measure requires community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services, not management and overhead. It authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance on qualifying expenditures and lets the Department of Public Health issue waivers. It authorizes monetary penalties and criminal charges. It is sponsored by a powerful labor organization seeking to expand its control over private clinics.
Vote NO on 44 .
YES on Prop. 45
Few things have impeded rational housing policy in the state more than the California Environmental Quality Act. It slows down development which, in turn, limits housing supply, increasing the cost of living. Far from being a tool to address legitimate environment concerns, it has been used more frequently as leverage by labor organizations to exact favorable labor agreements. While CEQA reform to prevent excessive delays is necessary, Proposition 45 is not perfect since it carves out only certain projects for reform and locks in costly labor agreements. It also creates opportunities for government to pick winners and losers. But while HJTA would prefer a full revamp of CEQA, Prop. 45 is a good first step.
Vote YES on 45 .
LOCAL BALLOT MEASURE RECOMMENDATIONS
City of Los Angeles
NO on Measure FD
This is a one-half percent sales tax increase in the city of L.A. with the revenue earmarked for the fire department. We oppose this measure because the sales tax in Los Angeles will already rise to 10.25% in October because of Measure ER passing in L.A. County in June, and because the City Council and the Mayor should fully fund the fire department from the existing budget of approximately $15 billion without a tax increase. This measure is a special tax that should require a two-thirds vote to pass, but courts have allowed “citizens’ initiative tax increases,” placed on the ballot by collecting signatures, to pass with fewer votes. HJTA’s ballot measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Proposition 43 on the November ballot) will close the loophole, but this tax increase, if approved by just 50% plus one vote, will squeeze through it before Proposition 43 takes effect in January.
City of Santa Monica
NO on Measure ES
This is a parcel tax, an extra $495 per taxable parcel of property every year, adjusted annually for inflation. The revenue is earmarked for schools. Special taxes are required by the constitution to be approved by two-thirds of voters, but this is another “citizens’ initiative tax increase” rushing to squeeze through the court-created “Upland” loophole before voters approve Proposition 43 in November.
City of Palos Verdes Estates
NO on Measure PVE
This is a renewal of a parcel tax with a massive increase in the per-parcel rate from $342 to $1,025 to pay for police services and “to pay down the City's unfunded accrued pension liability.” City voters previously rejected a different measure in June to renew and increase the temporary parcel tax.
El Dorado County
NO on Measure S
Measure S is a 30-year countywide sales tax increase. It would raise the sales tax by 3/8 percent. Marshall Medical Center is sponsoring the campaign for the tax. The Yes on S website states that “Marshall receives revenue to support $125M in bond issuance to fund capital improvements.” El Dorado County has only two hospitals: Marshall Medical Center and Barton Memorial Hospital. Measure S is structured so Marshall qualifies for the hospital funding while Barton does not. South Lake Tahoe residents would still pay the countywide tax even though Barton falls below the measure’s hospital eligibility threshold.
Five-County Bay Area
NO on regional transit sales tax
This is a sales tax increase of at least one-half percent (1% in San Francisco) in five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara) to fund transit. Critics rightly argue that the longstanding financial and management problems of transit systems in the Bay Area will not be fixed with another tax increase. Beyond that, a higher sales tax burdens people who already pay high sales taxes and are struggling with the high cost of living. This measure, too, is a “citizens’ initiative tax increase” attempting to get through the court-created loophole before HJTA closes it with Proposition 43.

California voters will decide in November whether to authorize two multibillion-dollar housing bonds — one to help fund new affordable homes and another to help buyers afford down payments on newly constructed properties.
One measure, Proposition 1, would let the state borrow $11.25 billion for a variety of housing efforts, including financing low-income apartments and providing low-interest home loans to veterans and first-time homebuyers.
The other, Proposition 37, would allow a state agency to sell up to $25 billion in bonds to lend money to homebuyers for down payments on newly constructed properties.
David Garcia, policy director at UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation, which does not take positions on ballot measures, said Prop. 1 would replenish crucial state programs to “continue building affordable housing throughout California.” He said Prop. 37, meanwhile, could help many residents who qualify for a mortgage but lack savings for a traditional 20% down payment, while also “creating demand for builders to build new housing.”
Opponents of Prop. 1, however, argue that while jumpstarting housing construction may be a worthy goal, it would be reckless for the state to take on billions in new debt while facing a long-term budget deficit. And although Prop. 37 is designed to pay for itself through buyers’ home loan payments, opponents fault it for not specifying how much borrowers would pay in interest and not prioritizing first-time buyers.
Neither measure would directly raise taxes, but Prop. 1 would need to be paid from the state’s general fund, potentially reducing money available for other services.
According to a recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) by the Public Policy Institute of California, 55% of likely voters support Prop. 1, while 61% support Prop. 37. Each requires a simple majority to pass.
Prop. 1
The largest chunk of Prop. 1 funding, $7.2 billion, would go toward state programs that provide grants and low-interest loans to developers to build affordable apartments and townhomes. Just over $1 billion would fund mortgage assistance for first-time homebuyers and other programs to encourage homeownership. Most of the remaining roughly $3 billion would support affordable housing programs for farmworkers, students and tribal members.
The bond funds would help subsidize up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, and provide as many as 40,000 households with mortgage assistance, home repairs and other homeowner support, according to the state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Chione Flegal, executive director of Housing California, a pro-housing group backing the measure, said tens of thousands of affordable units are now “shovel-ready” thanks to recent state laws that have rolled back development regulations. But with state housing programs running low on money, she said many of those projects need an additional funding source like Prop. 1 to break ground.
“You have both an incredible need and the conditions to actually get building quickly,” Flegal said.
In San Jose, a city-backed, 500-plus affordable housing development at 71 Vista Montana has faced years of delays after multiple attempts to develop it fell apart over funding issues, according to city officials. The City Council approved a new developer (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/03/san-jose-developer-city-land/) this month to move the project forward. Officials endorsed a plan for the developer to submit a financing proposal within three months, secure all funding within two years, and start construction within three years.

California voters last passed a dedicated state affordable housing bond in 2018, totaling $4 billion. In 2024, voters also approved $2 billion for homeless housing as part of a $6.4 billion mental health bond pushed by Gov. Gavin Newsom. Newsom, along with Democratic mayors and state lawmakers, has also backed Prop. 1.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which opposes the measure, argues it would be foolish for the state to take on new debt when it projects multibillion-dollar budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2026/5197/2026-27_Budget_Overview_of_Spending_Plan_082626.pdf) in the years ahead. If the state wants to support housing, it should find money already in its budget, which tops $350 billion this fiscal year, said spokesperson Susan Shelley.

OVERVIEW OF STATE BOND DEBT
PREPARED BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
This section describes the state’s bond debt. It also discusses how the bond measures on the ballot, if approved by voters, would affect state costs to repay bonds.
State Bonds and Their Costs
What Are Bonds? Bonds are a way that governments borrow money. The state government uses bonds primarily to pay for infrastructure projects that have a long useful life, such as bridges, dams, prisons, parks, schools, and office buildings. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects and then must repay the investors over a period of time, typically a couple of decades. This is very similar to the way a family pays off a mortgage on their home.
What Are the Costs of Bond Financing? The state’s total cost for a project is more if it pays with bonds than if it pays up front with money it already has. This is because it has to pay interest on the bonds. The amount of additional cost depends on the interest rate and how long it takes to repay the bonds. For example, if the state uses a 30-year bond with a 4 percent interest rate to pay for a project, the total cost is about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Most Bonds Must Be Approved by Voters. The State Constitution requires that most new bonds be approved by voters. These bonds usually are repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Bonds and State Spending
Current Amount of Bond Debt. The state currently is repaying about $80 billion of bonds from the state General Fund. In addition, the voters and the Legislature previously have approved about $40 billion of General Fund-supported bonds that have not yet been sold. Most of these bonds are expected to be sold in the next several years. The state currently is paying about $6 billion each year from the General Fund to repay bonds. The state will continue to pay a similar amount over the next few years. This is about 3 percent of the state’s annual General Fund revenue, which is lower than the historical average of about 4 percent.
This Election's Impact on Debt Payments. There are two General Fund-supported bond measures on this ballot: Proposition 1 and Proposition 38. Proposition 1 would allow the state to borrow $10 billion for affordable housing programs. The cost to repay this bond would be about $500 million to $600 million each year for 25 years. Proposition 38 would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. The cost to repay this bond would be about $500 million to $600 million each year for 20 years. The cost to repay both bonds would total about $1 billion each year, which is about one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the state’s annual General Fund revenue.

And effective altruist movement leadership tells me that their strongest opinion this year is to vote Scott Wiener for Congress in San Francisco. Wiener is a leader in AI safety and YIMBYism, and the California politics insiders I’ve talked to have been impressed by his intelligence, drive, and performance in Sacramento.
Here’s how I’m voting (Oakland, Alameda County, California):
I. California State Propositions
Proposition 1: Authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds to build affordable housing
Supporters claim it will build (or renovate) 40,000 homes; I asked an AI superforecaster (https://futuresearch.ai/) 1 to predict the true number, and it guessed that 22,000 would actually get built. That implies a cost of $500K per home, which would then be supplemented by state, local, and market funding for a total of $700K+ per affordable home. This is bad, albeit typical for California. Other things that turn me against this:
~5-10% will be spent on subsidizing demand, which will just drive up prices for everyone else.
~25% of the new homes are earmarked for specific groups like students, veterans, farm workers, and Native Americans, although this might not matter, since housing is fungible and those people will leave other houses that will then be available to the general public.
There are concerns that the government-sponsored-affordable-housing industry sometimes lobbies against market rate housing because it reduces the demand for government-sponsored affordable homes.
The AI superforecaster says that this would only decrease the cost of market-rate housing in California by 0.4%.
On the other hand, this is endorsed by CA YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/endorsements/) , YIMBY Action (https://yimbyaction.org/endorsements/november-2026-california-general?c=prop-1-bond-for-affordable-housing-ballot-measure) , and most other YIMBY groups, because we do need more housing. They claim this proposition is relatively well-designed by the low standards of California housing-related laws.
So it comes down to - given that California genuinely needs more homes, do we accept a standard California-style solution that gets those homes stupidly and expensively, or do we let the problem get worse in the hopes that maybe something magically changes later?
I weakly vote NO.
Proposition 2: Increases the state’s Rainy Day Fund
California makes much of its money by taxing the rich. The rich get much of their money from capital gains, which are high during booms and low during crashes. In 2014, California instituted a policy of saving money during booms that they could spend during the crashes, and this has gone well. But the original law was poorly designed and prevents the legislature from saving more than a certain amount, which was too low. Now they want permission to save a higher amount.
This seems like a rare bright spot of fiscal prudence. The opponents are mainly tax watchdogs who hope that if they make it harder for California to save money, California will have to give the money back to the taxpayers, which seems too galaxy-brained and irresponsible.
I vote YES .
Proposition 3: Extends an existing tax on wealthy people which is used to fund schools and health care
They say nothing is as permanent as a temporary tax increase, and in 2012, California voted for a temporary tax increase on wealthy people. It expires in 2030, and oops, now our entire budget depends on it and if we ever got rid of it then the schools would crumble into dust and the health system would be entirely replaced by witch doctors and shamans.
I do feel sorry for California’s budgetary officials, because our proposition system is constantly banning various categories of tax, and then they have to make up for it with other, sneakier categories of tax, including temporary taxes that become permanent. I believe everyone who says this would be devastating for education and health care if this were were allowed to expire. And honestly, I’m just happy to get a proposition that technically doesn’t put a new tax on me.
I weakly vote YES .
Proposition 4: Repeals prohibition on public funding of campaigns
California banned this practice in 1988, although the ban didn’t apply to a certain type of city called “charter cities” (not the same thing as Prospera (https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/prospectus-on-prospera) -style charter cities) which includes Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Oakland.
In the public funding model, candidates who get a certain number of small donors are eligible for public support for their campaigns, usually in the four-to-six digit dollar range. This supposedly makes it easier for ordinary people to compete with machine-backed candidates and billionaires. Opponents argue that taxpayers should not be forced to subsidize candidates they disagree with, and that these programs often become corrupt. Some considerations on this proposition:
It would probably cost about $75 million in extra local taxes, though not for me (Oakland already has this policy, so nothing would change).
It doesn’t invoke the state’s ethics watchdog, which would be the usual enforcer, strengthening concerns about local corruption. The San Francisco Chronicle opposes it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php) on this basis.
Studies suggest that public financing programs like these cause more candidates to enter, but that these additional candidates don’t win. There is no evidence that they make the incumbent win less, or reduce donor power.
The main study which does find a change in winning candidates finds that (https://stanforddpl.org/papers/hall_public_funding_2014/hall_public_funding_2014.pdf) it makes candidates more ideologically extreme, although other studies disagree (https://www.jstor.org/stable/24643820) .
Cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Oakland which currently have this policy under the charter city exemption don’t seem to be noticeably better.
The main countervailing consideration is that I don’t like when the state bans cities from trying things.
I weakly vote NO.
Proposition 5: Changes the California recall election process
A recall election is like an impeachment by the voters. If enough voters sign a petition, there’s a special election where we vote to get rid of an official (most often the governor). This special election also includes a list of candidates for who replaces him if he does get recalled.
Proposition 5 would keep the recall vote, but instead of a simultaneous vote to replace the official, the official would be replaced according to normal procedure: a recalled governor would be replaced by the lieutenant governor, other major officials would be picked by the governor, and legislators would be replaced in a special election.
The current recall system tends toward the following annoying equilibrium: every election, California picks a mildly corrupt pro-dysfunctional-establishment Democrat; a year later, the Republicans object that the candidate is mildly corrupt and in bed with the dysfunctional establishment, and gather enough signatures to hold a recall election; a year after that, the election happens, everyone spends millions of dollars sending billions of spam email messages, and then it fails, because the electorate just got done electing the governor and hasn’t magically changed its mind.
This proposition might break the cycle: if the Republicans know with certainty that the mildly-corrupt-pro-establishment Democratic governor will just be replaced by the mildly-corrupt-pro-establishment Democratic lieutenant governor, maybe they’ll stop trying this. And it preserves the useful part of the recall system: if the governor ever crosses the line into being so crooked that people would genuinely prefer the mildly-corrupt-pro-establishment Democratic lieutenant governor, we can still recall him.
The main argument against is in the San Francisco Chronicle: Proposition 5 Has A Flaw So Bizarre Even Its Author Doesn’t Like It (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php) . The flaw is that it says that the recalled legislator can run in the special election to replace themselves.
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds through donors. Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
According to the Chronicle , “[Proposition author Senator Josh] Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision. ‘I’m honestly not sure,’ he said.”
I don’t have a strong opinion on this, so I will trust the Chronicle . I weakly vote NO .
Proposition 37: Takes out $25 billion in bonds to help people afford down payments on housing
I vote NO.
Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology research
The great thing about California is that it’s not just a state where a few big special interests can money-pump the public. Anyone, no matter how small or humble, if they try hard and believe in themselves, can become a special interest that money-pumps the public.
Proposition 38 gives $8.4 billion of taxpayer money to immunology research, especially institutes that meet a list of qualifications. Only one institute meets the qualifications, and it’s the linked to the people backing this proposition. I see nothing else special about this research institute, and although immunology research in general is good, it’s not notably better than other good things that need money.
I strongly vote NO.
Proposition 39: Voter ID law
This is part of the national discussion about voter ID requirements. It mandates that California in-person voters show an ID, and that mail-in voters include the last four digits of an ID number (for example, Social Security).
There is generally little voter fraud in California elections. But this isn’t a law of nature: the last widely-agreed fraudulent US Congressional election was in 2018 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_North_Carolina%27s_9th_congressional_district_election) (although it was discovered and the result was annulled), and part of the reason that elections are so clean is that past generations took fraud risk seriously. 36 US states and most other developed countries request or require an ID to vote, this is standard, and not doing so feels a little like refusing to lock your door because you’ve heard there isn’t much crime in your area. Election integrity worries many people, I don’t think they’re all operating in bad faith, and I’d like to give them fewer things to potentially start a civil war about.
I appreciate that some people are bad at getting IDs, but these people are presumably already locked out of driving, getting alcohol, buying guns, most banking, and all other ID-requiring activities. We’ve decided that keeping these things secure is important enough that it’s worth inconveniencing people who are bad at getting IDs, and I don’t think voting security is any less important.
Prop 39 opponents additionally argue that the proposition is bad insofar as it creates a “private right of action” - that is, private citizens can sue if they think their county isn’t complying with this, and maybe this would choke the court with frivolous lawsuits. Supporters argue that in a Democrat-controlled state like California, the election officials are never going to enforce this, so they need a way for someone else to do it. I asked the AI superforecaster how many groundless lawsuits it expected from this proposition (defined as “lawsuits that got dismissed”). It answered a median of 3, 90th percentile estimate of 8.
I weakly vote YES.
Proposition 40: The billionaire wealth tax
This is the best-known and most hotly-contested initiative this cycle. It imposes a “one-time” 5% wealth tax on billionaires to fund state programs, mostly health care. Celebrity left-wing economist Gabriel Zucman supports. Opponents say that nothing is as repetitive as a one-time wealth tax, that it distorts the economy by forcing founders to prematurely sell stakes in their companies, that it will make billionaires leave California, and that it’s a particularly egregious case of using private citizens as a piggy bank for randomly-selected nice-sounding causes. It’s also sponsored by the SEIU, which is notorious for sponsoring ballot initiatives to extort (https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/seiu-delenda-est) groups they don’t like.
I asked the AI superforecaster to predict the outcome. They said that it would produce about $60 billion in one-time revenues and make enough billionaires move away to decrease the state’s permanent tax base by $2 billion yearly, and that if it passed there was a 33% chance of another wealth tax passing by 2046.
These numbers are about midway between boosters’ claims and opponents’, but based on the arguments in the first paragraph and at the linked post, I still vote NO .
Proposition 41: Bans state taxes that ignore the Gann limit
Voters like new taxes on billionaires, but hate new taxes on themselves. So a group of billionaires unhappy about the Proposition 40 billionaire wealth tax above figured they could write a proposition that sounds like it’s banning taxes in general - maybe even some especially dangerous and irresponsible form of taxes - but is mostly just banning Proposition 40. You don’t need to know what the Gann limit is except that Proposition 40 ignores it, and ignoring it sounds bad.
According to California law, if two mutually contradictory propositions pass during the same election cycle, whichever gets the most votes wins out. So if the voters who think that “taxes which ignore the Gann limit” sounds sinister outnumber the voters who think that “let’s seize the billionaires’ money” sounds fun, the wealth tax fails. Hooray for democracy!
I’m against the wealth tax, but this is kind of scummy. I weakly vote NO .
Proposition 42: Bans retroactive personal property taxes
Just in case Proposition 41 didn’t work, they also sponsored Proposition 42, another one which secretly sinks the wealth tax. “Retroactive personal property tax” is just another name for a wealth tax. If more voters oppose wealth-taxes-under-another-name than support wealth taxes, the wealth tax measure will fail.
I was more tempted to support this one than Proposition 41, because banning future wealth taxes really does seem like a good idea (one major concern about Proposition 40 is that the specter of a recurring wealth tax, regardless of whether it happens, will drive away rich people and chill economic activity). But it turns out this doesn’t work; future California voters can always repeal propositions passed by past California voters with a 50% + 1 majority, so new wealth taxes will face no electoral hurdle. All this will do is cancel the Proposition 40 wealth tax from this current election.
I weakly vote NO .
Proposition 43: Requires two-thirds majority for new local special taxes
Part of the eternal war between Californians voting for new taxes and Californians trying to ban themselves from voting for new taxes.
Although California does vote for too many new taxes, this law is an imposition of state power over local electorates, plus I will be voting for some of these ad hoc local taxes in this election (see Measure RTM), so it would be hypocritical of me to ban this.
I vote NO .
Proposition 44: Restricts community health clinics’ spending
This one is this election cycle’s SEIU extortion attempt.
If you haven’t been following along (https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/seiu-delenda-est) , the SEIU-UHW is a California union infamous for demanding that people give them money and concessions, then, if they don’t, sponsoring ballot propositions that would destroy their business.
This time around, they demanded some loot from community health clinics, those clinics didn’t cave, and the result was this proposition.
I strongly vote NO .
Proposition 45: Cuts environmental review requirements for new construction
This is the most YIMBY measure on this ballot, maybe the most YIMBY measure of the decade. It would significantly reduce the power of CEQA, one of the environmental review regulations that delays construction projects and new housing across California.
Most of the YIMBY groups I previously trusted, including CA YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/) and YIMBY Action (https://yimbyaction.org/endorsements/november-2026-california-general?c=prop-45-modify-environmental-review-for-critical-infrastructure) , have declined to take a position on this measure - which is shocking, since it’s far more aligned with the YIMBY spirit than the spend-taxpayer-money-on-affordable-housing proposition that they endorsed. The only explanation I can find is that this permitting reform would also make it easier to build suburbs and roads, and institutional YIMBYs can’t decide whether they hate suburbs and roads more than they like housing. I hope this isn’t the real reason, as it would significantly lower my respect for these groups and decrease my trust in their recommendations going forward.
I strongly vote YES .
II. California State Officials
I’ll be copying some of these from my discussion of the same races on my primary ballot.
Governor
As effective altruists, we are called to care for all creatures, from slimy shrimp to bodiless AIs, and so we may - perhaps - try to cultivate a tiny measure of compassion for California politicians. They face the near-impossible task of governing a state whose residents are allowed to kneecap them however they want through a bonkers ballot proposition system. If they try to build houses, a thousand local NIMBY groups will rise up to thwart them; if they don’t, the voters will kick them out for letting housing become unaffordable. If they tolerate homeless people and criminals, the voters will remove them for failing to prioritize public order; if they don’t tolerate them, the voters will remove them for cruelty and unfairness.
Having given them this small measure of sympathy, we can admit that Californian politicians mostly fail to live up to even the very low baseline we can fairly expect from them. They spend most of their effort maintaining a money spigot going to labor unions, prison guard unions, teachers unions, big donors, and anyone else whose support is necessary for their re-election.
Re-electing Democrats perpetuates this system and makes one complicit in it. If the Californian Republican Party took advantage of the situation by nominating moderates who disaffected Democrats can vote for with good conscience, all would be well. Instead, the average Republican challenger is mostly interested in bootlicking Trump as hard as possible, Stopping The Steal (as if we’re one election integrity law away from the GOP taking California!), and spreading various lies and conspiracy theories. They are against the infinite-money-spigot only insofar as they regret that it goes to Democratic donors and not to Big Agriculture, B

Quantifying the Impacts of Proposition 1
Published On: September 1, 2026 By California Housing Partnership (https://calhousingpartnership.org/author/chp/)
Proposition 1: The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026
California is the fourth-largest economy in the world, yet the lack of housing affordability remains a persistent challenge and a major driver of the state’s high poverty rate. 1 Not coincidentally, the state invests only a tiny fraction of its budget in creating more affordable housing. Between 2019 and 2024, California invested an average of only 0.8 percent of the annual state budget to affordable housing. 2
This November, California voters can significantly accelerate progress towards housing affordability by approving Proposition 1 and fast tracking more than 40,000 shovel-ready affordable rental homes and help 20,000 California households realize their dream of affordable homeownership. Proposition 1 will invest $11.25 billion into housing and put affordable homes within reach for working families and essential workers, from teachers and nurses to firefighters, and open the door to homeownership to first-time buyers. It will also build and preserve homes for Californians hit hardest by the housing crisis, including veterans and their families, people with disabilities, farmworkers, college students, foster youth, and seniors on fixed incomes.
Increasing Affordable Rental Homes
Proposition 1 will invest $11.25 billion to make housing more affordable across California, including $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program ( (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp#po-main-title)MHP (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp#po-main-title)) (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp#po-main-title) to build and rehabilitate 21,000 affordable rental homes for veterans, families and seniors, and $1.15 billion to create more than 3,500 affordable homes for Californians experiencing or at risk of homelessness. With more than half (54%) of renter households spending over 30% of their income on rent, these investments will expand the supply of rental homes that Californians can afford.
Putting Homeownership Within Reach for Veterans and First Time Homebuyers
At a time when only 19 percent of California households can afford the state’s median-priced home, 3 Proposition 1 will put homeownership, and the stability and opportunity it provides, within reach for more Californians, especially veterans. Proposition 1 will do this by investing $1.25 billion in the CalVet (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) program to expand homeownership for 3,700 veterans, $600 million to help 3,000 lower-income households build and own new homes through CalHome (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/calhome#po-main-title), and $500 million to assist 16,000 families buy their own homes using downpayment assistance through MyHome (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm).
Fighting Displacement
Proposition 1 will also make a major investment in preserving 3,200 affordable homes and preventing displacement of the low-income families and seniors who live there It will do this by investing $750 million in the Portfolio Reinvestment Program (PRP (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/prp#po-main-title)) to rehabilitate aging affordable housing, making critical repairs and improvements and another $200 million to establish a new Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program (CAPP) to protect existing residents from displacement by speculative investors buying up older apartment buildings.
Assisting Rural and Tribal Communities
Proposition 1 will also fund housing solutions for 2,500 farmworker families and members of California’s tribal communities in need. It will do this by investing $450 million in the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Grant Program (FWHG (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/fwhg#po-main-title)) to build and improve affordable homes for agricultural workers and their families, and $200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program (THGP (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/tribes/thgp)) to address housing needs in California’s Tribal communities.
Helping Governments Pay for Housing Infrastructure
Prop 1 provides another $500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program (IIG (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/iig#po-main-title)) to fund the creation of the streets, utilities, and infrastructure needed to unlock new development in our communities. Another $200 million will be invested in the Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/lhtf#overview)) Matching Grant Program to match locally raised housing dollars, allowing communities to leverage state funds for innovative solutions tailored to local needs.
Making College More Affordable Through Student Housing
Finally, Prop 1 will also provide $350 million through the Higher Education Student Housing Grant Program (HESHGP (https://www.cccco.edu/About-Us/Chancellors-Office/Divisions/College-Finance-and-Facilities-Planning/Affordable-Student-Housing/affordable-student-housing-program-information)) to create 1,400 affordable student homes. Homes funded through this program will remain affordable in perpetuity, benefiting an estimated 40,000 students over the next 55 years, with generations more in the future.
Making Every State Dollar Go Further
Affordable housing is financed through multiple funding sources, and the state bond pays a fraction of the cost of each home. Among developments receiving Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and bond investments between 2019 and 2025, state bond funding contributed an average of about $117,500 per affordable home, just 19% of total development costs. By comparison, approximately 58% came from private financing, 12% from local and regional sources, and the remaining 11% from other sources. In this way, state bond funding serves as a catalyst, unlocking substantially more public and private investment to get affordable homes built.
Reaching More Than 1.4 Million Californians
The impact of Proposition 1 will extend beyond the homes it builds and preserves. Over the next 55 years, more than 500,000 households, or 1.4 million Californians, are expected to benefit from affordable homes created and preserved through the measure, equivalent to roughly four percent of California’s current population.
Delivering $13 Billion in Rent Savings for Californians
Proposition 1 will help families keep more of what they earn. By building homes with rents well below market prices, the measure is expected to save California households nearly $500 million in rent each year once the housing is built. Over 55 years, these savings are valued at an estimated $13.2 billion, more than the bond’s $11.25 billion upfront investment. In other words, the rent savings alone are expected to exceed the bond’s total investment, even before accounting for broader economic and community benefits.
Improving California’s Future by Increasing Jobs, Wages, and Resiliency
These investments will ripple through California’s economy. These homes are expected to create more than 29,000 jobs and support approximately $1 billion in wages, salaries, and business income, while generating an estimated $300 million in annual state and local tax revenue. By helping more Californians afford to live near jobs, schools, and transit, Proposition 1 will reduce emissions, improve health outcomes, and build stronger communities.
Proposition 1 is a lasting investment in California’s future. With more than 40,000 affordable homes ready to move forward, it will put resources to work now, expand opportunities for homeownership, and strengthen communities across the state. The benefits will last for generations, helping more Californians afford to build their lives and futures here.
Jessica Hitchcock
Managing Director, Research
California Housing Partnership
Matt Alvarez-Nissen
Research Manager
California Housing Partnership
Lisa Tran
Equity Policy Research Fellow
California Housing Partnership
For questions about Proposition 1 impacts, please contact Jessica Hitchcock, CHP Research Director, at jhitchcock(at)calhousingpartnership(dot)org
Notes
(1) Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC), “California’s High Housing Costs Increase Poverty,” August 13, 2021.
(2) Annual state funding includes ongoing housing resources authorized through the state budget or permanent state law, including General Fund appropriations, dedicated special funds (such as SB 2), revolving housing funds, and the state Low-Income Housing Tax Credit.
(3) California Association of REALTORS, California Housing Affordability Retreated in the Second Quarter After Reaching a Four-Year High in Early 2026, August 5, 2026.

INTRODUCTION
Each year, our office publishes the California
Spending Plan to summarize the annual state
budget. In this publication we provide an overview
of the 2026-27 budget package, give a brief
description of how the budget process unfolded,
and then highlight the major features of the
budget approved by the Legislature and signed
by the Governor. This publication reflects the
administration’s estimates of legislative actions
taken through the end of June 2026. In addition to
this report, we will release a series of issue-specific,
online posts that give more detail on the major
actions in the budget package.
BUDGET CHOICES
In most years, we would describe the size of the
budget problem (or budget surplus) the Legislature
addressed (or allocated) and the mix of choices
that make up that total. This year, neither framing
fits the budget package as neatly. Although the
budget package includes some traditional budget
solutions, it also reflects a substantial amount of
new discretionary spending and a large, first-time
deposit into a surplus holding account. Taken
together, these choices roughly offset one another.
At the same time, the budget continues to rely on
reserve capacity, even as revenues have surged to
levels only surpassed by the state’s previous peak
in 2021-22. Taken altogether, this makes the budget
condition difficult to describe concisely. As such,
this section describes the state’s budget choices
on both sides of the ledger: first new commitments
and discretionary choices, and then the budget
solutions made.
NEW COMMITMENTS
Revenue and Spending Commitments
New Discretionary Spending Totals Nearly
$6 Billion. The budget commits $5.7 billion
in new, discretionary General Fund money in
2026-27. We define discretionary spending as
new spending or revenue reductions that were
not previously authorized under current law or
legislative policy. Nearly all of these commitments
are spending related—revenue reductions account
for only about $25 million of the total, mainly a
temporary reduction in the minimum franchise
tax for newly formed businesses. For context,
this new discretionary spending is equivalent to
roughly 90 percent of the total year-over-year
growth in General Fund spending between 2025-26
and 2026-27. A list of the discretionary General
Fund spending actions (excluding Proposition 98
(1988)) in the 2026-27 budget package are listed
in Appendix 1.
Most New Spending Is One Time, but the
Budget Also Added New Ongoing Costs.
Of the $5.7 billion in new discretionary spending,
about $5 billion (87 percent) is one time, while the
remaining roughly $700 million reflects ongoing
commitments—costs that will recur as part of
the budget’s baseline in future years. On a fully
phased-in basis, these will total about $825 million
annually. This new ongoing spending is a relatively
small share of the total. Nonetheless, it adds to the
budget’s baseline costs in future years, offsetting
the solutions described elsewhere in this report that
were used to address the gap between the state’s
ongoing revenues and expenditures.
New Spending Is Concentrated in Health,
Though New Spending Touches Nearly Every
Program Area. With over 250 individual items,
new discretionary spending reaches nearly
every part of the budget, but on a programmatic
basis, health programs account for the largest
share (nearly 40 percent of the total), followed
by general government, labor, and related
programs (15 percent); housing and homelessness
(12 percent); and criminal justice (11 percent).
Human services and resources and environment
programs each account for about 8 percent
to 9 percent, with the remainder split between
higher education (3 percent), K-14 education
(excluding Proposition 98) (2 percent), and
L E G I S L A T I V E A N A L Y S T ’ S O F F I C E

transportation (1 percent). Within health, the largest
commitments are two one-time actions that delay
previously planned reductions to Medi-Cal safety
net clinic and dental payments ($1 billion and
$258 million, respectively), along with $361 million
for dental benefits for adults with unsatisfactory
immigration status (UIS) and $250 million in public

outside of health include: (1) $400 million for the

program (HHAP); (2) $228 million for new child

Discretionary Reserves and Set Asides
Sets Discretionary Reserve Balance to
$4.5 Billion. The Special Fund for Economic
Uncertainties (SFEU) is a general-purpose
reserve commonly used to provide capacity for
unanticipated expenditures, including state costs
associated with disasters and other emergencies.
On a technical basis, it can be thought of as the
end balance of the state’s General Fund—the
money that remains after accounting for all of
the state’s expected revenues and spending.
The State Constitution has a balanced budget
requirement, which means the balance of the SFEU
must be set at zero or above for the upcoming
fiscal year (2026-27). Any level above that is up to
the discretion of the Legislature. As a result, we
consider the entire balance of the SFEU to be a
discretionary choice. The budget sets the SFEU
balance at $4.5 billion, in line with recent budgets,
which have set the balance between $3.5 billion
and $4.5 billion.
Makes $6.4 Billion Transfer to Temporary
Surplus Holding Account (TSHA). The budget
package deposits $6.4 billion into the TSHA, to
be withdrawn in 2027-28. Importantly, neither our
office nor the Department of Finance considers
this account to be a reserve. That is because, while
it can help the state manage surging revenues
within the budget window, it cannot mitigate
against a future downturn in revenues. The box
below describes this account and the transfer
in more detail.
What Is the Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA)?
Revenues Are Both Volatile and Uncertain. State revenues are volatile—they can grow or
shrink rapidly from year to year, particularly because California’s tax system relies heavily on
high-income taxpayers. This means that, in some years, the state will collect significantly less in
tax revenue than needed to cover its spending commitments—resulting in large budget problems.
Relatedly, there is significant uncertainty about near-term revenue estimates—that is, even for the
upcoming fiscal year, revenues can come in significantly above or below projections, resulting in
large forecasting errors. This is especially common when revenues are growing or shrinking rapidly.
TSHA Was Set Up to Avoid Overspending a Surplus. In 2024, the Legislature created the
TSHA as a tool intended to manage near-term revenue uncertainty. The account was designed for
periods when the state has a surplus driven by rapid revenue growth and might otherwise commit
to new spending based on revenue estimates that later prove overstated. The Legislature initially
considered establishing formulas or rules governing deposits into the account. Ultimately, however,
the TSHA was enacted as a flexible and largely discretionary mechanism.
Budget Uses TSHA for the First Time. The 2026-27 budget package deposits $6.4 billion
into the TSHA and plans to withdraw the same amount in 2027-28. (By law, funds can remain in
the account for up to one year.) In effect, this transfer uses anticipated 2026-27 resources to help
balance the following year’s budget, rather than allocating those resources to new purposes in the
current budget window.

I read the official guide, the LAO analysis, the bill text, polling, and editorials on both sides.

**The measure:** It authorizes $11.25B in bonds. About $10B is repaid from the General Fund. The LAO puts that at $500–600M a year for about 25 years, roughly 0.25% of the budget. The other $1.25B funds CalVet home loans that veterans repay themselves. It would subsidize up to about 40,000 rental units, plus some homebuyer, farmworker, student, and tribal housing. It creates no new tax, and repayment comes out of the General Fund.

**Best case for yes:**
- Earlier housing bond money has run out.
- About 40,000 permitted affordable units are reportedly stalled for lack of gap financing.
- The money leverages federal tax credits and private capital.
- It passed the Legislature 29–2 and 61–7.
- YIMBY groups, SPUR, and the SF Chronicle back it.

**Best case for no:**
- RAND found subsidized housing in California costs about 1.5× market-rate, and critics say the bond does little about why.
- Forty thousand units is only about 4% of the affordable homes the state needs, by the Mercury News's math.
- It adds to about $80B in existing bond debt, during a structural budget imbalance per the LAO.
- Only 11% goes to veterans, despite the title.
- Howard Jarvis, the Mercury News/East Bay Times editorial boards, and LA Times columnist George Skelton oppose it.

**Rule of thumb:** If subsidized affordable housing is worth about $550M a year in debt service to you, even at high per-unit costs, that points to yes. If you'd rather not add debt, or want the cost drivers fixed first, that points to no. If you tell me which matters more to you, I can say which way it points.
